HISTORY AND PHYSICAL NOTE

History:
• Presenting complaint: Wheeze and shortness of breath.  
• Onset / duration: Began ~2 days ago after vacuuming a dusty carpet; gradual onset ~1 h after exposure.  
• Progression: Persisting and worsening, particularly at night. Now short of breath while talking and occasionally unable to finish sentences.  
• Associated symptoms: No chest pain on deep inspiration, no dizziness, no fever or cough reported. Hydration adequate (≈4–5 glasses water/day).  
• Known triggers/exposures: Heavy dust exposure while cleaning house; history of seasonal hay-fever.  
• Previous episodes: Childhood asthma; occasional exertional wheeze as an adult.

Past Medical History:
• Childhood asthma (intermittent adult symptoms; keeps an inhaler).  
• Seasonal allergic rhinitis/hay-fever.  
• Previous steroid use for asthma (details not provided).  
• Allergies: Denies known drug or food allergies.  
• Medications: Old asthma inhaler (type/dose/route/frequency not documented); no regular antihistamines or other medication.  
• Surgical / hospital history, family history, social history (smoking/alcohol): Not recorded.

Physical Examination:
• General appearance, vitals, respiratory exam: Not recorded (video connection with limited/no exam performed).  
• Mental status: Alert and conversant.  
• No reports of tongue or throat swelling.

Impression:
Likely allergen-triggered asthma exacerbation.  
Alternative considerations (consistent with transcript):  
1. Acute dust-mite allergic reaction with lower-airway involvement – dust exposure, atopy history.  
2. Viral bronchitis – less likely; no infectious symptoms.

Management Plan:
• Advise patient to attend nearby GP/urgent clinic today for in-person assessment: pulse oximetry, peak-flow, and full respiratory exam.  
• Suggest over-the-counter oral antihistamine en-route (if available) pending evaluation.  
• Inform that systemic corticosteroids may be required, decision deferred until examination.  
• Letter to GP prepared and sent via app summarizing presentation and requested assessment.  
• Educate on monitoring: seek immediate care if breathing worsens, speech becomes impossible, or chest tightness develops.

Patient Summary:
40-year-old woman with childhood asthma developed progressive wheeze and dyspnoea 2 days after heavy dust exposure at home. Presentation most consistent with an asthma flare possibly triggered by allergen. She is being referred for same-day in-person evaluation with instructions to initiate antihistamine and await possible further treatment.

Key Takeaways:
• Attend GP/urgent clinic today for oxygen saturation and lung function testing.  
• Obtain and take one OTC antihistamine as soon as possible.  
• Return or seek emergency care if breathing deteriorates or you cannot speak full sentences.

Next Steps:
• In-clinic: vital signs, pulse oximetry, peak-flow, consider short-acting bronchodilator trial, and decide on oral steroids.  
• Consider prescription of regular preventer inhaler and allergy management after acute episode.  
• Schedule follow-up to review asthma control and need for action plan.
